The Stratospheric Controlled Perturbation Experiment (SCoPEx), proposed by Harvard University and led by Frank Keutsch, aimed to investigate aerosol behavior in the stratosphere to improve computer models evaluating the risks and benefits of solar geoengineering, particularly solar radiation management. Importantly, SCoPEx was not intended to deploy geoengineering or cool the planet but to analyze aerosol microphysics and chemistry by releasing a minimal quantity of calcium carbonate (between 100 grams and 2 kilograms) at altitudes around 20 km using a scientific balloon gondola.

A planned test in Sweden in 2021 was limited to hardware checks, as the SCoPEx Advisory Committee recommended postponing the release of particles until further societal engagement could be achieved. In March 2024, it was announced that Keutsch would no longer pursue SCoPEx, with the platform expected to be repurposed for other stratospheric research. Ozone depletion and the chemical consequences of various aerosol types remain critical concerns in the ongoing discussion surrounding solar geoengineering research.
